newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Mined highway to greet Afghan rebels.
newsitem.headline: Mined highway to greet Afghan rebels.

text.p: Afghan government forces have mined the main eastern Kabul-Jalalabad highway to stop any more advance by the rebel Taleban militia to the strategic town of Sarobi, military sources said on Sunday.

The move follows last week's fall of the strategic eastern province of Nangarhar and the adjoining Laghman province's capital of Mehtar Lam to the Islamic militia seeking to take maximum territory in its drive to topple President Burhanuddin Rabbani's government in Kabul.

A senior government delegation has left for Uzbekistan capital of Tashkent for talks with powerful northern Afghan warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum to persuade him to join Rabbani's administration, a government spokesman said in Kabul.
He said Iranian deputy foreign minister Alaeddin Boroujerdi was also due to arrive in Kabul later on Sunday after talks with Dostum in the northern Afghan town of Mazar-i-Sharif.
Sarobi, about 60 km (37 miles) east of the capital Kabul, is the government's last eastern base on a plateau that overlooks the Kabul-Jalalabad road.
The location of two hydro-electric plants, one of which is planned to begin supplying power to the war-shattered capital soon, has added to the importance of Sarobi town of more than 20,000 people.
A narrow road also links the township to the Afghan government main airbase at Bagram, north of Kabul, through the Tagab valley to the north.
The government frontline is a 30-km (18-mile) long gorge, which, with high peaks on the two sides, is considered the main barrier against a Taleban assault on the town.
In addition, the government troops have laid anti-tank and anti-personnel mines on the road to stop the Taleban, military sources in the area said.

But the closure of the road, which is the main supply route from neighbouring Pakistan, has hit the civilian population of Sarobi and Kabul, with food and fuel prices having doubled in the past five days.

Most of the shops in Sarobi were closed on Sunday owing to the shortage of food and uncertainty prevailing in the town with Taleban militia threatening to attack it after last week's chain of victories in eastern Afghanistan.
Some families have already left the area, fearing the outbreak of fighting in the town, residents said.
"I am leaving for Kabul. We are not certain about the future of the town, said Ehsan (one name), head of a six-member family while loading his belongings on a truck.
He said many families had already evacuated the area.

Several tanks, armoured personnel carriers and trucks mounted with anti-aircraft machineguns, had crammed under the shade of pine trees as reinforcements of confident-looking soldiers headed for the frontline.
"We will soon launch a counter-attack on Taleban from three directions," a government commander said.

He said an advance on the main eastern town of Jalalabad, the Nangarhar province capital taken by Taleban on Wednesday, would be made from Tangi-e-Abreshum (Silk gorge), Alising valley in Laghman province and from Kunar province, north of Jalalabad.

Military analysts said Taleban would find it hard to make any further westward advance from Jalalabad to Sarobi as the militia forces would be very vulnerable and exposed if they tried to pass the gorge.
A military spokesman in Kabul confirmed earlier Taleban reports that government jets bombed Jalalabad on Sunday.

"The compound of the governor's palace as well as the airbase of Jalalabad were bombarded each two times by one plane," said Amrullah, spokesman for the Kabul government's top military commander Ahmad Shah Masood, told reporters.
The Afghan government accuses Pakistan of helping Taleban. Pakistan denies the charge.
